gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1019r:
How the Pentagon buys commercial satellite bandwidth is the focus of GAO-05-1019R, a letter of September 27, 2005, that sends a Senate briefing to the record. The Department of Defense gave Congress its own report on that buying process on July 29, 2005. The Senate Armed Services Committee asked GAO to grade it.

GAO checked the Pentagon report against seven fixes from its own December 2003 study. Staff gave the results to the committee on September 2, 2005. The letter sums up that briefing and passes it on in full. Readers get a scorecard on whether defense satellite buying had tightened up as urged.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1029r:
Post-Hearing Questions Related to Agency Implementation of the Improper Payments Information Act, GAO-05-1029R of September 16, 2005, holds written replies to a Senate panel. GAO had testified on July 12, 2005, about wrong federal payments. The law at issue, passed in 2002, makes agencies hunt for plans at risk of big payment errors. It also makes them post yearly error sums.

Senators sent fresh written queries on August 24, 2005. The replies draw on GAO's check of agency reports for fiscal year 2004. They show which agencies did the risk checks the law demands. They also show the error sums agencies owned up to that year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-309r:
Health and Human Services' Estimate of Health Care Cost Savings, GAO-05-309R of February 17, 2005, is a letter that picks apart one big claim. U.S. health care cost an estimated $1.7 trillion in 2003. It is a maze of paper, phone calls, and split records. Tech could trim waste and lift care. The health department put a sum on those gains.

Congress asked how that sum was built. GAO traces its steps and its base facts. It splits the sum to show what share would fall to the federal purse. The letter sits in a wider study of the push for a national health tech plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-319r:
Management Report, GAO-05-319R of March 10, 2005, checks how a tax site guards the cash and facts that flow through its mail room. The Brookhaven campus in New York was the first tax site to shrink its paper return work in fiscal year 2004. More folks file by wire each year. The shrink cut the load of checks and forms the site must guard.

Congress asked for the check as a guide for sites that will shrink next. GAO reads the rules Brookhaven wrote for safe care of mail and data. It tests the locks in use. It gives fixes for Brookhaven and for the sites to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-389r:
Consolidation Loan Borrower Interest Rates, GAO-05-389R of February 25, 2005, is a short letter with one point to make. A House chair asked if a past GAO tip still holds. The tip, from an October 31, 2003 report, was to weigh a shift in school loan merge rates. Merge loans let past pupils fold old school debt into one loan. Their rate now sits fixed for the loan's life.

A rate that floats with the market could cut the federal cost of the plan, GAO said then. Time has passed and rates have moved. The chair asked if the tip still stands. It does, the letter holds: a float rate stays a live path.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-499r:
In GAO-05-499R (June 10, 2005), GAO passes on the audit report for the American War Mothers, covering its fiscal year ended August 31, 2003. The corporation aids men and women who served in the World Wars or other U.S. conflicts. It gives special help to those who were wounded or left unable to work.

Chartered corporations must present their assets, debts, income, and costs in yearly statements. They must also pay an independent accountant to audit those statements. GAO's task was narrow: to flag anything in the report that broke the financial reporting rules in the law. Its staff read the statements and notes and applied simple analytical checks. Nothing that broke the rules came to light. The auditor's view was that the statements fairly presented the group's finances under standard accounting rules. GAO stresses that it did not itself audit the books.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-509r:
The Marine Corps League's audit reports for two years are the matter of GAO-05-509R, a letter dated June 10, 2005. The league fosters interest in the Marine Corps and fellowship among all Marines. It also serves the survivors of Marines who have died. The years covered ended June 30, 2003, and June 30, 2002.

As a federally chartered corporation, the league must present yearly statements of its finances. Those statements must be audited by an independent public accountant. GAO read the statements and the auditor's report and ran basic analytical checks on the figures. Its aim was to advise the House Judiciary Committee of any reporting problem. None was found that needed reporting. The auditor's opinion was that the statements were fairly presented under generally accepted accounting principles. GAO returned the audit reports with its letter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-529r:
Proposed changes to how rates are set for flying U.S. mail abroad are weighed in a GAO letter, GAO-05-529R, dated April 8, 2005. The Transportation Department sets what the Postal Service pays U.S. carriers to fly letter-class and military mail overseas. The method dates from a rate case that closed in the late 1970s. A Senate postal reform bill would change that process.

GAO found the bill's rate provisions fit its guiding ideas for postal change. Those ideas balance freedom to act, efficiency, and fairness. The bill would let the Postal Service bargain over rates and services with U.S. and foreign carriers. Other clauses guard fairness. One shields contractors, and one phases in foreign carrier competition over 5 years with a reciprocity rule. GAO cautioned that new freedom must come with oversight. That pairing, it said, keeps the service fair to customers and rivals alike.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-589r:
The Tennessee Valley Authority's representation letter for fiscal year 2004 is reviewed in GAO letter GAO-05-589R, sent on June 23, 2005. The power authority's letter forms one piece of the audit trail behind the government's yearly financial statements. GAO tested it against five key areas from the federal audit manual. Two of the five needed work, the review found.

No materiality thresholds came with the letter. Without them, the Treasury cannot weigh the authority's figures as it builds the government-wide letter. The letter also held only 21 of the 26 standard representations that applied. One further item was partial, and 4 were absent altogether. GAO judged the gaps easy to close. It made two recommendations to the authority's chief financial officer. A third went to the inspector general, who was asked to work with the authority and its outside auditors on future letters. The authority's finance chief commented on the draft.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-599r:
For the Department of Veterans Affairs, GAO's review of the fiscal year 2004 representation letter is GAO-05-599R, dated July 22, 2005. The letter supports the audit of the government's consolidated financial statements. It records what VA leaders confirmed about their own books. GAO tested the letter in five key areas and found faults in two of them.

The letter carried 25 of the 29 standard representations that applied to the department. Three of the other 4 were partial, and 1 was missing. The department also sent an incomplete summary of the misstatements it had left uncorrected. GAO said the faults could be easily addressed. It made two recommendations to the acting chief financial officer, each aimed at a specific fix. The inspector general, working with the outside audit firm, was asked to help with future letters. Both the finance chief and the inspector general agreed with the recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-609r:
A 2003 letter is the subject here: the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund's, covered by GAO-05-609R on July 22, 2005. Even an older letter feeds the government's consolidated audit chain. GAO found one of five key areas wanting. The fund's letter carried 22 of the 25 standard representations that applied. Three were missing in full.

GAO told the National Credit Union Administration's finance chief to include them all in future letters, and asked the Acting Inspector General to help, with the outside audit firm. The finance chief agreed with the advice, while noting that one of the three items seemed to have been provided after all.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-649r:
A menu of Social Security fixes, with no picks made, is GAO letter GAO-05-649R of May 6, 2005. It gathers every generic reform device found in recent plans the program's own actuaries have scored. Options run from raising the retirement age to new benefit formulas and tax changes. Variants are merged: lifting the age to 68 or 70, or tying it to longevity, count as one device with many settings.

Each entry is weighed against GAO's standing test for reform plans: lasting solvency, fairness, and how well benefits match contributions. A companion list names the scored plans behind the menu.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-659r:
Early doubts about a Pentagon mobility study are raised in GAO letter GAO-05-659R, sent September 14, 2005. The study will guide buys of airlift planes, tankers, and sealift ships, all resting on computer models. GAO is shadowing the work at the Senate's direction and must judge the final report within 30 days of its release. Its core worry: the department barely documents how it verifies, validates, and accredits those models.

Weak paper trails make the study's claims hard to trust or repeat. GAO wrote early so the flaws can still be fixed, and it lists changes for this study and future ones.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-679r:
Guarding the money markets against cyber attack is checked in GAO letter GAO-05-679R, dated June 29, 2005. GAO probed seven key market bodies: exchanges, clearing houses, and payment processors. All had the five parts of a sound security program, from written policy to access controls. Each still had fixes to make against hackers, viruses, and insider misuse. Most fixes were done or planned by the time of writing.

The two market regulators were briefed in detail and said they would track the work. The letter withholds the weak points themselves, for safety.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-699r:
Did community policing grants cut 1990s crime? GAO letter GAO-05-699R, June 3, 2005, gives an interim account. The 1994 law set aside $8.8 billion and aimed to add 100,000 officers. The grants went to state and local law enforcement agencies. By 2001 grants of $7.3 billion were promised and about $5 billion spent, near 1 percent of local police budgets for the period. Violent crime fell steeply in the same years, and one recent study credits the grants with part of the drop.

This letter reports where GAO's own test of that claim stands and how it is built. Final judgment waits on the full study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-799r:
NASA's finance system upgrade gets a status report in GAO-05-799R, dated September 9, 2005. The space agency began the program in April 2000. It aims to fix deep flaws in money management and reporting. In 2003, GAO issued four reports on the effort. They warned the agency had skipped key best practices. Those reports carried 45 recommendations.

GAO found some progress since then. The agency has moved to gauge risk in joining system parts. It has also sharpened how it tracks defects and tests changes. But a full enterprise design to guide the work is still limited. No plan exists to cut the risk of relying on parts already in use. Core finance needs are not yet fully written down. A full life-cycle cost estimate is also still missing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-839r:
Admin costs of support programs are compared in GAO-05-839R, a letter dated June 30, 2005. Billions flow each year to programs that aid low-income families. A large share covers administration, not direct aid. GAO examined a set of such programs. It counted total funding and split out admin spending by type. It also gathered the federal matching rates for those admin costs.

The letter puts the programs side by side on shared terms. Readers can see how much of each program's money goes to running the program itself. They can also see how much of that admin bill Washington picks up. The comparison gives Congress a base for asking whether admin shares are in line across programs with like aims.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-909r:
Follow-up answers on the Paperwork Reduction Act make up GAO-05-909R, a letter dated July 19, 2005. GAO had testified on June 14, 2005, about the act. It discussed the budget office's yearly burden report and its own study of agency practice. Congress sent further questions on June 22, 2005. This letter answers them for the record.

The questions concern the act's rules on information collections. Those rules govern how agencies seek data from the public and how burden is counted. The answers add detail to the June hearing record. Readers get GAO's reading of the burden estimates and of agency compliance work in one place. The letter pairs with the testimony and the underlying GAO study of the act.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-999r:
The tax watchdog inside Treasury is itself reviewed in GAO-05-999R, a letter dated September 27, 2005. The office audits and investigates the tax service. A 1998 law created it as an independent inspector general. Congress asked GAO to review its work. GAO covered its budget and staff, its coverage of the tax service, its results, its quality checks, and how its advice is followed up.

Over fiscal years 2000 through 2004, the office's budget rose 14 percent while staff fell 6 percent. In fiscal year 2004, it held about $130 million and 877 full-time staff. Its audit plans mirror the tax service's own structure and cover its management challenges. In 5 years, it issued 942 audit reports. It handled 39,611 complaints and closed 22,350 investigations, it reported.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-139r:
Outreach for the Medicare drug discount card is described in GAO-06-139R, a letter report dated November 18, 2005. The 2003 Medicare law told the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to spread word of the card widely. Millions of seniors and people with disabilities could use the card and its aid for low-income users. The agency ran ads, mailings, and help lines to publicize the card and aid enrollment. Congress asked GAO to review those efforts, since the new drug benefit was set to start in 2006.

GAO described the education campaign and weighed outside reviews of it. Research groups in the public and private sectors had graded the effort. GAO also reported enrollment figures for the card program. It named factors that may have held enrollment down. The card was a short bridge to the full drug benefit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-159r: GAO-06-159R is a letter report dated October 7, 2005. It records GAO's review of audit reports for the National Music Council. The reports cover the council's financial statements for fiscal years 1993 through 2001. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance in any of those years. The auditors' opinions held that the statements were presented fairly. They were prepared in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The letter is brief and states the result in plain terms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-199r:
Aviation trust fund taxes get a records check in GAO-06-199R, a letter report dated November 4, 2005. The Airport and Airway Trust Fund collects excise taxes that help pay for the nation's air system. GAO helped the Department of Transportation judge whether the net tax sum sent to the fund for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2004, rests on solid records. The work followed a set of procedures the two sides agreed in advance.

The checks ranged wider than a single year. GAO reviewed the tax agency's quarterly certifications for the fund and Treasury adjustments booked in fiscal year 2005. It tested early receipt figures for two quarters of that year. It also probed the tax office's methods for estimating fourth-quarter sums. Key matches between tax and Treasury records closed the work. The letter reports what those agreed checks found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-229r:
Restated science agency books are examined in GAO-06-229R, a letter report dated December 22, 2005. GAO audits the government's consolidated statements each year. During the fiscal year 2004 audit, a worry stood out: more agencies were restating past statements to fix errors. The National Science Foundation restated its fiscal year 2003 figures. Errors can spring from math slips, wrong use of accounting rules, or missed facts.

This letter reports GAO's findings on the foundation's case. A recording error in the H-1B visa fee account forced the restatement. GAO urged the foundation's finance chief to fix the flaws behind that error. It also urged the inspector general to help auditors sharpen tests for such errors. The two officials replied with their views on how large the errors were. GAO clarified its stance on both points. The letter is one of a series on the restatement wave.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-279r:
Retired battleships and the fire support they once gave fill GAO-06-279R, a letter report dated December 13, 2005. Iowa class battleships backed beach landings with 16-inch guns through the 1991 Gulf War. The last one left service in 1992. Congress feared no equal shore fire support would arrive for decades. In 1996 it told the Navy to keep at least two of the ships on the register. They must stay until the Navy certifies an equal or better capability. The Wisconsin and the Iowa sit in reserve under that order.

GAO has reported on the ships' status several times since 1995. In November 2004 it found the Navy and Marine Corps had only just begun to set firm fire support needs. This letter updates that record. It weighs what the old ships can still offer against the cost of waking them. The debate joins nostalgia to hard questions about range, accuracy, and crews.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-299r:
A stopgap drug discount card and the firms that ran it are examined in GAO-06-299R, a letter dated January 13, 2006. The 2003 Medicare law added a full drug benefit that began in January 2006. To bridge the wait, it set up a temporary discount card program in June 2004. Cards gave Medicare patients discounts at the drugstore counter. Low-income patients without other cover could add a subsidy toward their drug costs. Private sponsors offered and managed the cards. The Medicare agency oversaw them.

This letter reviews how sponsors handled the program and its subsidy. Special cards targeted set groups, and some sponsors ran more than one card. Oversight mattered because public money rode on private handling. The review came as the bridge program wound down. Planners of future transitions can mine it for what to copy and what to avoid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-29r:
Annual reporting on military training ranges gets a mixed grade in GAO-06-29R, a letter report dated October 25, 2005. Troops must train as they intend to fight, GAO notes. Ranges are where that practice happens. Training has grown more complex, with services drilling together more often. Commanders report rising limits on realistic training. A 2003 defense law requires a yearly report on those constraints.

Some improvements have been made, GAO found. The report still falls short of what Congress required. As last year, it offers no ideas for legal or rule changes. The department sent its proposals in a separate paper in April 2004. GAO has long sought a full inventory of ranges and a clear plan to fix crowding. Costs, goals, and owners must be named for progress to be real. The letter keeps the pressure on a quiet readiness issue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-319r:
Counting America's defense trade, and the flaws in the count, is the work of GAO-06-319R, a letter dated January 27, 2006. Arms trade shapes the supplier base and the spread of key technology. It affects access to parts in wartime and teamwork with allies. Sound choices need complete and trustworthy data. The Senate armed services panel directed GAO to find and judge the data on hand. GAO listed the defense trade figures the government itself produces. It noted the limits of each source.

GAO then computed trade balances for 2000 through 2004 from those figures. Gaps and mismatches between sources cloud the picture. A balance is only as firm as the counting behind it. The letter gives lawmakers a map of what is known and what is guesswork. It matters because export policy debates often cite numbers as settled fact. Here the numbers come with their warning labels attached.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-359r:
Claimed savings in veterans' health care did not rest on firm proof. A GAO letter report, GAO-06-359R of February 1, 2006, checks the Department of Veterans Affairs. About 7 million veterans were enrolled for VA care in fiscal year 2005. VA planned to serve about 5 million of them. Its first budget request that year was $30.2 billion.

Budget plans for fiscal years 2003 through 2006 assumed large savings. Those savings came from management efficiency steps. Congress asked GAO to test the method behind the claims. GAO found only limited support for the reported savings. Readers learn how the figures were built and why they drew doubt.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-39r:
Survivors of Pearl Harbor keep a chartered group, and its audit drew one caveat. Letter GAO-06-39R, dated October 7, 2005, reviews the Pearl Harbor Survivors Association audit. The audit covers the fiscal year ended September 30, 2003. The group works to preserve and encourage study of Pearl Harbor history. Its focus includes records, mementos, and events tied to the attack.

GAO read the statements, notes, and auditor's report. It found no reportable instance of noncompliance. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly on a modified cash basis, with one exception. The auditor had not watched the physical inventory count. The group also posted an $11,689 prior period adjustment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-459r:
The market regulator's own accounting steps needed repair. A GAO letter report, GAO-06-459R of April 21, 2006, discusses internal control at the Securities and Exchange Commission. The letter follows GAO's November 15, 2005 report on the commission's fiscal years 2005 and 2004 statements. That report also covered internal control as of September 30, 2005. It included tests of compliance with selected laws during fiscal year 2005.

This letter's purpose is narrower. It sets out issues found in the audit that could be improved. The focus is internal controls and accounting procedures. Readers get the detailed findings behind the audit opinion. The record suits readers tracking financial reporting quality.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-469r:
A court monitor watched over a landmark settlement for Black farmers. Letter report GAO-06-469R, dated March 17, 2006, studies the Pigford settlement. In 1997, three African-American farmers sued the Department of Agriculture. They alleged the department denied or delayed their farm loan applications. A consent decree settled the class action on April 14, 1999. The court noted decades of discriminatory practice by the department.

GAO measured how much the court-appointed monitor took part in outreach. It also counted claims the monitor sent back for reexamination. It reports the results of those second looks. Readers get a focused view of one part of the settlement machinery.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-489r:
Retired service members gain a health supplement only if they join Medicare Part B. Letter report GAO-06-489R, dated June 30, 2006, studies TRICARE enrollment in Medicare Part B. TRICARE for Life began in 2001. It adds coverage for beneficiaries who have Medicare Part A and enroll in Part B. A 2003 law gave enrollment incentives to those who had missed their first sign-up window. Four federal groups shared the work of carrying out that law.

GAO describes steps each group took, including fixes for problems met. It measures how far beneficiaries were served by the incentives. Readers see a benefit that depends on paperwork across agencies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-509r:
Veterans who lost their sight have a group of their own, and its books were reviewed. Letter GAO-06-509R, dated March 14, 2006, covers the Blinded Veterans Association. The audit reports run for fiscal year 2003. The group's purpose is to promote the welfare of blinded veterans. It also promotes fellowship among them, as its charter states in the letter that GAO sent to Congress on this audit.

By law, such chartered groups must present their assets, debts, income, and costs in yearly statements. An outside public accountant must audit those statements. GAO read the statements and the audit report. It found no reportable case of failure to follow the law. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly under U.S. accounting rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-589r:
Every six months, GAO must count Haitian applicants gaining permanent residence. Letter report GAO-06-589R, dated April 21, 2006, is the fourteenth such report. The Haitian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act of 1998 set the duty. The act let certain Haitian nationals and their dependents apply to adjust status. Reports must break down applicants and approvals by category. Categories include asylum applicants, parolees, and children without parents. Orphaned and abandoned children are listed too. Dependents such as spouses and children also count.

Reports continue until all applications are finally decided. Readers get the running tally in a set format. The value lies in the series, which tracks the act to its end.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-599r:
Knowing what a program costs is a basic tool of management, and agencies vary at it. Letter GAO-06-599R, dated April 18, 2006, sums up a briefing on managerial cost accounting. The briefing covered the Department of Health and Human Services and the Social Security Administration. It was the third in a series on large agencies. Earlier briefings covered Veterans Affairs, Labor, Education, Transportation, and the Treasury. Laws and standards require agencies to build cost information systems.

GAO studied how agencies generate cost information. It also studied how managers use that information for decisions and accountability. Congress asked how far agencies develop and use such data. Readers get two agencies' practices in brief.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-689r:
Mining history has a federal audit check in GAO-06-689R, a GAO letter dated May 12, 2006. The National Mining Hall of Fame and Museum is a federally chartered corporation. It keeps a library and museum that collect and preserve the history of mining in the United States. Chartered corporations must present yearly financial statements under federal law. An independent public accountant must audit them.

GAO reviewed the audit reports for the museum's fiscal year 2003 statements. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance with the law's financial reporting requirements. The auditor's opinion said the statements were presented fairly under United States accounting principles. GAO's letter reports that result to Congress. The review is brief, but it closes the oversight loop for that year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-699r: Post-hearing questions got GAO answers in 2006, and the letter carries the responses for the record. The findings deliver the answers. The letter keeps the oversight loop closed. The questions got their answers. The oversight loop stayed closed. The record stayed complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-69r:
State payments for Medicaid prescription drugs are compared in GAO-06-69R, a letter report dated October 31, 2005. Drug coverage is an optional Medicaid benefit that every state and the District of Columbia chose to offer. Spending on outpatient drugs had become a substantial and growing share of Medicaid costs. GAO compared how five states paid pharmacies for the same drugs. GAO also checked how each state's payment level matched its own formula for estimating drug cost.

GAO found minimal variation among the five states' payments for most drugs. Payments for 189 brand-name drugs varied by less than 7 percent on average. Payments for the five generic drugs reviewed varied by 30 percent on average. Payment levels lined up with each state's cost formula. The study gives a factual base for drug pricing debates.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-739r:
Oversight of military supply vendors is faulted in GAO-06-739R, a letter report dated June 19, 2006. Under the prime vendor model, one distributor supplies a product line to military customers in a region. In fiscal year 2005, prime vendor sales were about $9 billion of the Defense Logistics Agency's $32 billion in total sales and services. GAO reviewed how the Defense Supply Center Philadelphia checked vendor prices.

GAO found that staff did not always run required pricing reviews. Medical goods and food commodities got regular price checks. But reviews were missing for food service equipment and for construction and equipment goods. Long-running contracts in those areas went without the checks. GAO said attention was needed to improve oversight, so the military does not overpay for supplies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-789r:
How Navy ships are powered is surveyed in GAO-06-789R, a letter report dated July 6, 2006. The Navy uses nuclear propulsion for its submarines and most aircraft carriers. Surface combatants and amphibious ships rely on conventional systems that burn fossil fuel. As the Navy designs a future force it can afford, old assumptions face review. Fuel cost, endurance, and ship design all turn on the propulsion choice.

The letter lays out the propulsion options for ships and submarines. It reviews the factors that guided past Navy choices, such as speed, range, and life-cycle cost. GAO suggests some of those assumptions may need a fresh look. The letter was sent to the House subcommittee that oversees projection forces. It gives lawmakers a primer for future shipbuilding debates.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-89r:
Official U.S. presence at government-backed public policy forums is surveyed in GAO letter GAO-06-89R, dated October 21, 2005. The government backs thousands of conferences and seminars each year. They let U.S. and foreign crowds debate policy and learn official U.S. views.

Congress asked how far U.S. officials took part in such forums. GAO covered forums backed by the Departments of State, Defense, Energy, and Interior from 2001 through 2004. It measured official turnout at those events. It also listed each department's rules for sending officials. The letter shows how public forums serve, or miss, their stated policy aims.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-959r:
Follow-up answers on charities and taxes are sent in GAO letter GAO-06-959R, dated July 7, 2006. The letter replies to a House subcommittee chair. It grows out of a May 25, 2006 hearing on whether charities in the Combined Federal Campaign meet their job tax duties.

GAO based its answers on its audit work for that hearing. It also drew on talks with the Internal Revenue Service. Its views rest on accounting and audit norms, and on its own judgment. The letter is short and narrow by design. It puts GAO's post-hearing answers on the record, so the subcommittee file on campaign charities is complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-999r:
Screening of contract staff who serve deployed troops is probed in GAO letter GAO-06-999R, dated September 22, 2006. The Defense Department counts more than 50,000 contract workers in Afghanistan and Iraq. They fix weapons, run networks, guard gates, translate, cook, and wash clothes.

Such staff can also pose risk, as the attack on the U.S.S. Cole showed. Checks can flag past crime and deter some threats, though the department need not screen them. In Iraq it used body-based checks. GAO found the checks may lack key facts. It also noted steps U.S. forces take to curb the risk that stays.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1029r:
Two costly space systems, and the Defense Department's use of proven build steps, are covered in GAO letter GAO-07-1029R, dated August 2, 2007. A satellite network called TSAT would give fast, secure links worldwide. Space Radar would watch the earth in all weather, even in barred zones.

In 2004 TSAT life costs were put at about $16 billion. Space Radar was put at $20 billion to $25 billion. Both face huge software work and deep tech hurdles. Congress asked GAO to grade the use of best practice as builds near. The letter sums up March 2007 briefings: gains made, hurdles kept.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1139r:
A Navy call to back one personnel system over a joint one lacks fair proof, GAO states in letter GAO-07-1139R, dated July 25, 2007. In June 2006 the Navy weighed the Marine Corps' pay and personnel system, MCTFS, against a joint system, DIMHRS. It chose the Marine system. The Defense Department had spent over $668 million on the joint one by September 2006.

A 2007 defense law told the Navy to report on its choice, with cost tests and fit checks. The Navy held the two near equal in cost, and its pick less risky. GAO reviewed that report for a ruling due no sooner than 120 days after April 25, 2007.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-209r:
Farm inspectors at the border moved to a new department, and many told GAO they were unhappy. Their views fill GAO-07-209R, a letter dated November 14, 2006. More than 1,800 agriculture specialists moved from the Agriculture Department in March 2003. They became border protection staff with an antiterror mission. Congress feared farm safety checks might lose focus. GAO surveyed the specialists and analyzed their written answers.

The written answers pointed to morale problems, GAO found. Comments on what should change ran to 185 pages. That was about 4 times the volume on what was going well. The second most common answer on the bright side was that nothing was going well. Specialists felt the farm protection mission had been weakened by the move. Their answers matched the survey's scored questions. The letter lists the five most common themes for each open question.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-239r:
Medicaid pays pharmacies for drugs under a federal price cap that was about to change. GAO estimated the new cap's bite in GAO-07-239R, a letter dated December 22, 2006. From January 1, 2007, the cap rests on average manufacturer prices. Budget officials expected the change to save $3.6 billion from 2007 to 2010. Pharmacies feared the cap would fall below their buying costs. GAO tested that fear on 77 common and costly drugs.

The new caps would sit below average pharmacy costs for 59 of the 77 drugs, GAO found. Across the sample, they ran 36 percent lower on average. For high-spending drugs, they ran 65 percent lower. The gap could shrink if pharmacies bought cheaper versions or won price cuts. The Medicaid agency disputed GAO's methods and findings. GAO stood by its data as the best available at the time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-329r: GAO-07-329R, dated January 26, 2007, covers the National Woman's Relief Corps, Auxiliary to the Grand Army of the Republic, Inc. GAO reviewed the audit reports on its financial statements for fiscal years ended August 31, 2005 and 2004. The auditor found the statements presented fairly on a modified cash basis of accounting. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance in its review.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-339r:
A new federal loan guarantee for clean energy technology launched before its risk rules existed. GAO flagged the haste in GAO-07-339R, a letter dated February 28, 2007. A 2005 energy law created the program. It backs loans for projects that cut pollution or use new technology. Projects must show a reasonable prospect of repayment. GAO reviewed start-up funding and risk exposure. It also checked the Energy Department's management steps.

The department spent about $503,000 to start the program through October 2006, GAO found. The money paid three detailed staff and support contracts. Guidelines went out and project pitches came in quickly. But core policies were missing. Rules for picking lenders, pricing the subsidy, and tracking loans were not set. Program goals lacked outcome measures. GAO listed five steps to finish before any guarantees are picked. The department generally agreed with the findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-409r:
Money left unspent on finished building projects is the focus of GAO-07-409R, dated May 9, 2007. The General Services Administration (GSA) builds and leases space for federal agencies. Its projects can run for years, so leftover funds carry over between years. GSA must spot funds that are no longer needed and shift them to other work.

GAO asked whether GSA had ready data on these balances across its building accounts. It found that GSA lacked fast, sound data on project status. Rules to flag spare funds were weak. The sums found were small next to the whole budget, but bigger amounts could pile up unseen. GAO gave the GSA chief three steps to fix tracking and to show carryover funds plainly in budget requests. Congress, GAO noted, needs that clear view.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-469r:
The General Federation of Women's Clubs had its books checked, and GAO-07-469R, a short GAO letter of March 9, 2007, reports the result. The club federation is a federally chartered corporation. Its aim is to better communities through volunteer work in art, education, conservation, home life, and public affairs. Under 36 U.S.C. 10101, such bodies must file yearly financial statements and get an outside audit.

GAO read the audit reports for the fiscal years ended June 30, 2005 and 2004. It ran checks on the figures and read the auditor's report. GAO did not audit the books itself and gave no opinion of its own. It found no breach of the law's reporting rules worth reporting. The auditor held that the statements were fairly presented under standard accounting rules. The letter closes the yearly oversight loop for this charter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-659r:
Extra answers on the Interior Department's troubles arrive in GAO-07-659R, a GAO letter dated March 28, 2007. On February 16, 2007, GAO testified at a House Natural Resources oversight hearing. The hearing weighed reports by GAO and the department's inspector general. On February 26, 2007, committee members sent follow-up questions about GAO's past reports. This letter answers them.

The replies rest on work already published, plus GAO's wider store of knowledge on the department. GAO did not seek the agency's comments on the draft, since no new audit work stands behind the answers. The topics reach across the department's sprawling brief: land, energy, parks, and tribal trust among them. Like other letters of its kind, this one exists to complete the hearing record. Staff writing oversight bills draw on it as a cited source.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-669r:
Former lawmakers keep a chartered association, and its audit is reviewed in GAO-07-669R, issued April 5, 2007. The Former Members of Congress works to promote good government at the national level. It aims to deepen public grasp of Congress as an institution and to strengthen public support for it. As a federally chartered corporation, it must present yearly financial statements in detail and obtain an outside audit.

GAO's letter covers the fiscal year ended December 31, 2005. Staff read the audit report, the statements, and the notes, and ran checks on the numbers. They did not audit the association or render their own opinion. The review found no instance of noncompliance worth reporting. The auditor's opinion held that the statements were fairly presented under standard accounting rules. The letter is brief, matching the slim file of a small membership body.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-689r:
GAO-07-689R, a management report dated May 11, 2007, lists control flaws GAO found at the Internal Revenue Service. The flaws came up in GAO's audit of the agency's fiscal year 2006 financial statements. They touch tax data, receipts, refunds, penalties, liens, and gear. None of the points had open recommendations from past audits. GAO set out 21 new recommendations in the report.

At three of four lockbox banks, backup files with taxpayer data were not coded for safety as rules demand. At two of six campuses, cameras missed parts of the grounds. Staff who gave manual refunds did not always watch accounts to stop double payments. The agency sent refunds to some taxpayers who owed payroll taxes. Errors also hit penalties, lien releases, and fees for payment plans. Each flaw raised the risk of loss or misuse of taxpayer data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-809r:
Rebuilding on the Gulf Coast is surveyed in GAO-07-809R, a letter GAO sent on June 29, 2007. The 2005 hurricanes wrecked homes, roads, and businesses across the region. Hundreds of thousands of people lost their homes. Nearly two years later, some towns still lack schools and hospitals. Many shops remain shut. GAO briefed Congress several times on its early work in Louisiana and Mississippi. This letter transmits the facts shared at those briefings.

The letter puts federal aid to date in the frame of total resources. Big choices loom on levees, coastal restoration, and land use. Who pays for each project is a key open question. Some neighborhoods will need rebuilding from the ground up. That work could take decades in places. GAO calls this a turning point for the recovery. Its full studies of the effort were still under way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-829r:
Oil and gas work on wildlife refuges is reviewed in GAO-07-829R, a letter dated June 29, 2007. The refuge system covers 95 million acres in every state. The federal government owns most of the surface land. Private parties often own the mineral rights below it. Those owners may drill for oil and gas on refuge land. GAO's 2003 report found oversight of that work needed repair. This letter checks how far the Fish and Wildlife Service has come since then.

Pressure to drill on federal lands has grown with energy demand. The 2003 report flagged doubt over the service's power to require access permits. It also found land-buying guidance unclear. The service and the Interior Department took steps on GAO's past advice. Gaps in oversight and management remain, GAO found. The letter weighs which past recommendations are done. It also marks where firmer rules could protect refuge wildlife and habitat.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-899r:
Security controls at the Bureau of the Public Debt are reviewed in GAO-07-899R, a letter dated June 14, 2007. The bureau manages the federal debt schedules that GAO audits each year. GAO judged its controls effective overall for fiscal year 2006. As part of that audit, GAO tested computer security over key systems. It found matters that fall short of reportable conditions. They still merit management attention and action. This letter presents those issues in public form.

Testing found eight new security control issues. Seven involve general controls, such as access rules and software change control. One involves reporting of unusual activity in an application. Physical security and activity monitoring softened the risks. Of 11 older recommendations, 8 had been completed by September 30, 2006. Three access control fixes were still in progress. GAO made eight new recommendations in a limited-use version. The bureau said work on most points is under way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-929r:
Sales of sensitive military gear to the public are rechecked in GAO-07-929R, a letter dated July 6, 2007. The Defense Department sells surplus through a contractor's website. Items marked for destruction must never reach that site. Past failures let F-14 parts slip through to buyers. Iran flies F-14s and hunts for such parts. Congress asked GAO to test the fixes. GAO watched the sales flow for about seven months.

Controls have improved a great deal, GAO found. In September 2006, 295 destruction-marked items still sold. Later bad listings were caught and withdrawn before sale. Crews removed 59,762 lines of sensitive stock before sale in eight months. Those lines held 1.3 million single pieces. New steps include tighter lot building and release checks. A post-sale retrieval process now exists as well. Some property was newly classed as controlled. The letter credits the cleanup while noting the early lapse.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-999r:
A transport aid program for people with disabilities is reviewed in GAO report GAO-07-999R, issued July 19, 2007. The New Freedom program funds services beyond what the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 requires. The Federal Transit Administration runs it. Congress gave the program $77.2 million in fiscal year 2006 and $81.0 million in fiscal year 2007.

GAO found that progress in getting the program running has been limited. Grant funds flow through bodies named by state governors. Slow starts left much of the new service still to come. GAO also found weak oversight of the funds. It urged better monitoring so grant money is spent as Congress intended.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1149r:
A highway partnership statement is enclosed in GAO letter GAO-08-1149R, issued September 8, 2008. The letter sends Congress a statement drawn from a GAO report of February 2008. That report studied deals in which private firms help finance and run highways. Such deals are growing across the country.

The statement weighs the gains, costs, and trade-offs of these deals. It reviews how officials have tried to guard the public interest in them. It also looks at the federal role and how that role might change. The core message is plain: more rigorous analysis upfront could better secure the gains and protect the public.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-19r:
School mental health services and the federal role in them fill GAO letter GAO-08-19R, dated October 5, 2007. A 1999 surgeon general's report found that about one in five U.S. children has a mental health problem that can impair daily life. Many of those children get no care. Schools host much of the care that does exist.

The letter describes the work of the federal mental health agency in this field. That agency teams with the education and justice departments on a joint school initiative. It also joins a wider partnership on child mental health. GAO weighs what helps or hinders schools in giving such care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-439r:
The Defense Department's civilian workforce plan is judged in GAO letter GAO-08-439R, dated February 6, 2008. The department's civilian staff numbers almost 700,000 people. Over half will be eligible to retire within a few years, which could drain skills the mission needs.

The law ordered a strategic plan for this workforce, but GAO found the plan sent to the Armed Services Committees fails most of the law's requirements. It does not spell out skill gaps or the recruiting and retention tactics to close them. Without those parts, Congress cannot judge the hiring effort, and the future workforce may lack key skills. GAO recommended that the Secretary of Defense order a fresh plan that meets the law, sent to Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-819r:
Written answers after a January 31, 2008 hearing fill GAO-08-819R, a letter dated June 20, 2008. The hearing, called Eliminating Agency Payment Errors, probed how agencies meet a 2002 law on bad payments and a duty to audit for overpayments they can claw back.

The answers report where agency efforts stand, program by program. Named programs include a military health benefit program and a family aid program. Lawmakers asked how risk checks, error counts, and recovery audits are coming along across the government. Readers get the follow-up record in one place, in GAO's own words to the subcommittee chair.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-849r:
Miners have taken billions in gold, silver, and copper from federal lands since the General Mining Act of 1872, with no royalty owed. Congress now weighs adding one. GAO-08-849R, a letter dated July 21, 2008, gathers facts on state royalties and on mineral trade trends.

Most hardrock mining sits in 12 western states. Those states do charge royalties on their own lands, plus taxes on digging. The letter lays out how each state charges, and how imports and exports of key minerals have moved. Lawmakers get a factual base for the royalty debate, drawn from state law and trade data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-919r:
Terrorism insurance for city buildings is the subject of GAO-08-919R, a July 2008 letter sharing early results. After the September 11 attacks caused about $32.5 billion in insured losses, insurers largely stopped selling terrorism coverage. Congress answered with the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002, reauthorized in 2005 and 2007, under which the federal government shares losses from future attacks. The 2007 law ordered GAO to study whether some markets still cannot get coverage.

The letter documents GAO's compliance with that reporting duty and encloses the slides from June 2008 briefings for committee staff. The slides cover whether availability is tight in any geographic markets, what the tightness does to prices and coverage amounts, and what limits insurers' willingness to write this coverage at all.
